[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Terraform Automation, Workspaces, and Environment Separation"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Managing infrastructure across multiple environments such as development, staging, and production is a core challenge in DevOps. Terraform provides native features like workspaces, alongside automation strategies, to handle this complexity effectively."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Terraform Workspaces"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Terraform workspaces allow you to maintain multiple distinct states within a single configuration directory. While they are useful for switching between different contexts, they share the same backend configuration, making them ideal for minor environment variations."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"# Create and switch to a new staging workspace
terraform workspace new staging

# List available workspaces
terraform workspace list

# Switch back to default workspace
terraform workspace select default"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Using Workspace Interpolation"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can use the terraform.workspace expression to dynamically alter resource naming or sizing based on the currently active workspace."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"
  instance_type = terraform.workspace == "production" ? "t3.large" : "t3.micro"

  tags = {
    Environment = terraform.workspace
    Name        = "Webserver-${terraform.workspace}"
  }
}"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Workspaces vs Directory Separation"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Workspaces share the exact same state backend configuration and credentials, differing only in the state file data."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Directory separation (e.g., /environments/dev and /environments/prod) is recommended for strict isolation, distinct security boundaries, or different cloud provider accounts."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Automating Terraform in CI/CD Pipelines"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"To remove human error, Terraform operations should be automated via CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins). Automation requires non-interactive execution flags."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"# Initialize without prompting
terraform init -input=false

# Automatically approve applies in pipelines
terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Enterprise Automation"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always use remote state backends (like AWS S3 with DynamoDB locking) for team collaboration and pipeline execution."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Incorporate automated policy-as-code tools like Sentinel or Checkov into your pipeline to scan Terraform plans before applying."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Never hardcode secrets; inject environment variables or use secret managers during pipeline runs."}]
